annual_update_corrections.changes_summary: Two changes to the plan since the 2025 renewal, both notified to Oregon Tilth in writing before they took effect. First, Grandevo WDG (Pro Farm Group, OMRI listed, EPA Reg. 84059-27) was added to the spotted wing drosophila programme on the three blueberry blocks as a rotation partner to Entrust SC. The materials-list update went to OTCO in writing on 12 February 2026, and the first application was 26 June. By our account OTCO acknowledged it on 26 February under ticket OT-26-01174; that acknowledgment is not recorded with the notification in Trazo. Second, Bottom Ground A carried two crops in 2026 instead of one: spring spinach closed on 8 June and a second carrot planting went in on 20 June, which changes the rotation for that parcel but adds no acreage. Native hedgerow maintenance on the Upper Terrace north edge continued under the NRCS EQIP 422 contract established in 2024. No input, parcel, practice or buyer has been removed since the 2025 plan. Everything else stands as filed: no new or removed parcels, no change to the certified acreage (86.9 acres across six parcels), no change of certifier, buyers or handlers, no livestock, and no change to the buffer arrangements on Home Field East, Home Field West or the Upper Terrace. As in 2025, the operation is a split operation with parallel production on its buffer rows: the west-edge blueberry rows on Home Field East and Home Field West are buffer rows under § 205.202(c), picked separately and sold as conventional fruit, as the plan's G6.0 answers describe.
annual_update_corrections.correction_note: Revision 3 corrects revision 2 (filed 1 October 2026) on four points. (1) Revision 2 said there was no split or parallel production. The operation is a split operation with parallel production on its buffer rows, as its plan's G6.0 answers say, and that has not changed since 2025. (2) Revision 2 listed three changes already made in 2026 under additions intended for the coming year. They are reported under (a)(1); no addition intended for 2027 is stated in this revision. (3) Revision 2 listed a statement about the past under deletions. It is now in (a)(1); no deletion intended for 2027 is stated. (4) Revision 2 said Oregon Tilth acknowledged the Grandevo materials update on 26 February under ticket OT-26-01174. No acknowledgment is recorded with that notification in Trazo, so this revision gives the date as the operation's account, not as a recorded acknowledgment. Revision 2 is kept as filed.

establishment.custom_message: Thanks for scanning. We have grown certified organic fruit and vegetables on this ground since 2006, all of it in real soil. Every pick and every input is recorded here as we do it.
establishment.description: Family-run organic farm on the Calapooia River in Linn County, Oregon, certified organic by Oregon Tilth since 2006 and Real Organic Project certified since 2020. Forty acres of soil-grown blueberries (Duke, Draper, Liberty) on sawdust-mulched raised beds, and fifty acres of rotation ground in carrots, onions and spinach with winter cover crops. Everything goes to wholesale: fresh fruit and vegetables through Organically Grown Company in Portland, process-grade berries to Willamette Valley Fruit in Salem.
establishment.irrigation_methods: ["Drip on blueberries","Drip tape on vegetables","Overhead sprinkler (frost protection and germination)"]
establishment.name: Calapooia Bend Farm
establishment.soil_types: ["Winter cover crops (cereal rye, vetch, crimson clover)","Purchased OMRI compost (Rexius)","Douglas-fir sawdust mulch on blueberry beds","Permanent grass alleys","Hedgerows and riparian buffer"]
establishment.split_operation_plan: Buffer rows only. The outside row (row 1) on the west edge of Home Field West, and on the north part of the west edge of Home Field East, sits against a conventional grass-seed neighbor, so under 7 CFR 205.202(c) its fruit cannot be sold as organic. Those rows are staked orange and marked on the block map, picked last on their own day into red-tagged lugs that touch nothing else, kept out of the organic cooler and pack line, and sold to Willamette Valley Fruit as conventional process fruit on a separate bill of lading under a lot code beginning CBF-CONV, with its own weigh ticket and sales record. No other non-organic product exists on the operation and no prohibited material is stored on the farm.
establishment.zone: Willamette Valley — Calapooia River bottom, Linn County

osp_change_notifications.description: Grandevo WDG (Pro Farm Group; OMRI listed; EPA Reg. 84059-27) added to the spotted wing drosophila programme on Home Field East, Home Field West and the River Block, as a rotation partner to Entrust SC. Rate 2 lb/ac in 100 gal/ac by airblast, applied at dusk after bee flight, REI 4 h, PHI 0 d. Added because relying on Entrust alone through a five-week pick window is a resistance risk (both are used in the same IRAC-conscious rotation). No other input, practice or parcel changed.

Bottom Ground A will carry a second crop in 2026. When the spring spinach closes (expected early June), carrots (Bolero F1, organic seed) will be direct-seeded on the same 18.6 acres. Same parcel, no added acreage; the rotation for this parcel changes for 2026. No input, practice or other parcel changes.

contract_notes.value: Brandt Family Farms LLC, an Oregon limited liability company, trading as Calapooia Bend Farm. The certificate is issued to Brandt Family Farms LLC; Calapooia Bend Farm is the farm name that appears on our bills of lading and on the buyer-facing pages, and both names are on file with Oregon Tilth. Laurel Brandt is the member-manager and the person responsible for this organic system plan. The operation holds 138.6 acres in Linn County, of which 86.9 acres across six parcels are in certified organic production — 37.7 acres of blueberries (Home Field East 12.5, Home Field West 14.0, River Block 11.2) and 49.2 acres of rotation ground (Bottom Ground A 18.6, Bottom Ground B 16.4, Upper Terrace 14.2). The balance is the riparian corridor along the Calapooia, the native hedgerows, the farmstead, the packing shed and the equipment yard; none of it is cropped. The only non-organic product is the fruit off buffer rows 1 and 2 on Home Field East and Home Field West, kept separate and sold as conventional process fruit as section G6.0 describes; no other crop on the operation is grown for the conventional market.

fraud_review_process.value: I review this myself each January when I put the renewal packet together, and again whenever something in the chain changes. The check is short because the chain is short: everything we sell is grown on our own six parcels and goes to two buyers — Organically Grown Company (OTCO-0042) for fresh, Willamette Valley Fruit for process. Before the first load of each season I pull both handlers' certificates and confirm they are current in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including that they have not been surrendered or suspended, and I do the same for any input supplier that is itself certified. Input labels and invoices are checked against the OSP materials list when the delivery lands, not later. The picking crew gets the organic-handling talk before harvest every year (see the June training record) because a seasonal crew is where separation actually gets tested — red-tagged buffer lugs, no personal produce in the field, clean lugs only. What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.

osp_accuracy_process.value: Laurel Brandt, the owner, keeps the plan accurate. There are two of us who touch the records: Javier Morales logs the field work in Trazo as it happens — every spray, every pick, every cleanout — and I review what he has logged before the renewal packet goes to Oregon Tilth. A change on the ground reaches the plan by that route: when Grandevo went into the SWD rotation this February, it was logged as an input, the materials list changed, and OTCO got the change notice before the first application in June rather than after it. Anything that changes acreage, a parcel, a buyer or a handler goes to OTCO the same way.

seedlings_description.value: The only transplants we buy are onion transplants (starts grown in cell trays) for the Upper Terrace and Bottom Ground B. They come from Calapooia Starts Co. in Brownsville, certified organic, grown from organic seed in their own greenhouse — 2026 lot PAT-26-TRANS-04 on invoice CSC-26-0771, organically managed from sowing on 15 January. We do not run a greenhouse of our own. Their organic certificate is pulled and checked before the order each spring and filed with the invoice.

planting_stock_description.value: The blueberry plantings are the only perennial stock on the farm. Home Field East (12.5 ac 'Duke') was planted spring 2006 with two-year bare-root plants from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, Lowell OR. Home Field West (14.0 ac 'Draper') was planted spring 2013 with containerised plants from the same nursery. River Block (11.2 ac 'Liberty') was planted spring 2016, containerised, also Fall Creek. No perennial stock has been established since 2016 and none is planned. All three blocks are on raised beds with Douglas-fir sawdust mulch and drip.

rotation_plan.value: The three vegetable parcels run a four-year rotation and never carry the same family twice running. Bottom Ground A: carrots 2025, spring spinach then a second carrot crop 2026, brassica 2027, then a full cover year. Bottom Ground B: onions 2025, carrots 2026, spinach 2027, cover 2028. Upper Terrace came out of a fallow/cover year in 2024 and went into onions in 2026 — it is the ground we rest when a block needs it. Every vegetable parcel carries a winter cover of cereal rye with hairy vetch and crimson clover, drilled behind the harvester in October and terminated in March or April. The blueberry blocks are perennial and are not rotated; biological diversity there comes from the permanent grass row middles, the hedgerow and the flowering understorey rather than from rotation.

tillage_practices.value: Vegetable ground only. In autumn the crop residue is flail-mowed and disced in and the cover is drilled the same week. In March or April the cover is flailed at rye boot stage and disced in two passes, then the beds are rototilled to about six inches and levelled with a Perfecta harrow for seeding — that is the deepest we go, and it happens once per crop. In season the only steel in the ground is the finger and torsion weeders either side of the rows and bed-middle sweeps, both shallow. Nothing is inverted, we do not plough, and passes run across the slope. The blueberry blocks are not tilled at all: the row middles are permanent sod that is mown, and the under-row strip is mulched with sawdust.

compost_initial_cn_ratio.value: About 32:1 — carrot and onion wash-line trim and spoiled straw against flail-chopped prunings and sawdust fines.

compost_temp_and_days.value: 131-147 F, held above 131 F for 16 days on the 2026 windrow (probe readings at five points per 100 ft, logged on the compost sheet).

compost_turnings.value: Five turnings within the 15-day period; the 2026 windrow had three by 25 August and finished the remaining two by 8 September.

raw_manure_timing_detail.value: No raw manure is applied anywhere on this operation, and none is kept on the farm. The rule above is recorded only because the question requires an answer; there is no raw manure practice to describe. Our nitrogen comes from cover crops, plant-material compost, feather meal and fish emulsion.

conservation_plan_detail.value: NRCS EQIP contract covering practice 422 (field border) — the 1,400 ft native hedgerow along the Upper Terrace north edge, planted 2024 with oceanspray, red-flowering currant, snowberry and native rose. The same contract covers the pollinator strip on the Bottom Ground A headland. Linn Soil and Water Conservation District advised on the riparian corridor along the Calapooia on the east side of Bottom Ground A, which we leave uncut.

irrigation_water_sources.value: One well (Well #1, 25 hp submersible at 85 ft) supplies the whole farm — drip on all six parcels, with overhead only for germinating the vegetable ground. No surface water is drawn from the Calapooia and we are not on an irrigation district.

water_quality_test_frequency.value: Annually before the season starts. Edge Analytical, Corvallis — 2026 report 26-W-0412 dated 20 May: generic E. coli <1 MPN/100 mL, nitrate-N 1.2 mg/L, pH 6.9.

input_use_conditions.value: Only when monitoring says prevention has not held, and only from the approved inputs list. On blueberries that means spotted wing drosophila: traps go up at green fruit and the first confirmed female once fruit shows colour is the action point, because SWD turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly threshold would be too late. The programme is then Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation, both OMRI listed, at four to five day pick intervals, applied at dusk after bee flight, with drops and culls buried the same day. Bloom disease is covered by Serenade Opti at about 30 percent bloom and again ten days later, only in a wet bloom. Surround WP goes on if we get a heat event at colour. On the vegetable ground no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied — weeds are handled by flaming, cultivation and hand crews. Nothing is applied while hives are on the block.

monitoring_records.value: Every scouting trip, trap read and threshold call is logged in Trazo against the block it belongs to, with the counts, what was found and what we decided — including the trips where we decided to do nothing, which are the majority. Trap positions are marked on the block map and the paper log sheet lives in the scouting binder in the office. The record for each application names the product, the rate, the area, the applicator and the REI and PHI.

drift_response_procedure.value: Stop harvest on the affected rows, isolate anything already picked, and photograph and note what was seen — wind, time, direction, the equipment on the neighbouring ground. Call Oregon Tilth the same day before any of that product moves, and follow their instruction on whether to test or to divert the block. Nothing from an affected area ships as organic until OTCO says it may. The neighbours on the north and west lines have standing written no-spray-without-notice agreements with us and both have honoured them since 2011.

containers_cleaning_method.value: The picking lugs are dedicated to organic fruit (buffer-row fruit goes into red-tagged lugs that are never used for an organic pick, section G6.0), and they are washed and sanitised before the first pick of each block: pressure wash, hand scrub, Tsunami 100 peroxyacetic acid at 80 ppm checked with test strips, then air dried on racks. The pack line is sanitised the same way the morning of each pack day. Both are logged as equipment cleanout records against the season.

non_own_transport_records.value: Organically Grown Company's reefer collects the fresh fruit. Every load leaves with a bill of lading carrying our lot code, the pallet count, the seal number and the words 'Certified organic — OTCO-1463', and the driver signs it. OGC returns a receiving report against the same lot. The trailer is pre-cooled and inspected before loading and the carrier attaches a cleanout affidavit naming the previous load. Willamette Valley Fruit collect the process fruit on the same terms, on their own separate BOL.

storage_cleaning_method.value: The cooler is emptied, swept, washed down and the floor and drains sanitised before the first fruit of the season goes in, and it is checked and wiped between crops. The onion shed is swept out and the forced-air fans and ducts cleaned before curing starts. Both are inspected by eye at the same time — for damp, for rodent sign, for anything left from the previous crop — and the check is written on the cleanout log.

handling_site.value: A single open-sided packing shed on the home place with a concrete floor, next to the two forced-air cooling tunnels and the cold room. The line is a wash tank and flume for the root and leaf crops, a roller sorting table, a grading belt and a clamshell filler for the fruit. The onion curing shed is separate, with forced-air fans. All of it is organic-only: buffer-row fruit never enters the shed, the cooler room or the pack line (section G6.0).

process_flow.value: Blueberries: hand picked into lugs, shuttled to the shed every 45 minutes, forced-air cooled to 34 F within two hours, tipped onto the sorting table, filled into clamshells, palletised with the lot code on the pallet tag, held at 34-35 F, shipped to OGC. Machine-picked tail fruit goes straight into totes and to Willamette Valley Fruit as process grade. Carrots: lifted, flumed and washed in well water, graded, packed 25 lb, cooled, shipped. Onions: lifted, field cured five days in the windrow, three weeks forced-air in the shed, topped, graded, sacked 50 lb. Spinach: band cut, flumed, iced and packed 20 lb the same day. Buffer-row fruit never enters this flow — it is picked separately into red-tagged lugs and goes out on its own bill of lading as conventional.

products_handled.value: Only what we grow: fresh blueberries in 12 x 1 pt clamshell flats, process blueberries in bulk totes, carrots washed and packed 25 lb, onions cured and sacked 50 lb, spinach washed, iced and packed 20 lb.

water_source_sanitizer.value: Potable water from Well #1, tested annually (Edge Analytical, 2026 report 26-W-0412). Tsunami 100 (peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide) is dosed in the wash flume at 80 ppm and checked with test strips; it is allowed under § 205.601(a)(6). No chlorine is used, and residual is not an issue because there is no chlorine rinse step.

sales_soe_channels.value: Wholesale only, two buyers. Organically Grown Company (Portland DC, handler certificate OTCO-0042) takes the fresh blueberries, the washed carrots, the sacked onions and the spinach. Willamette Valley Fruit takes the machine-picked process blueberries. We do not sell direct to consumers, we do not attend farmers' markets, and we run no CSA.

sales_soe_lot_linkage.value: Every sale carries the lot code from the season it came out of — CBF-26-HFE for the Duke block, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach, and so on. The lot is on the bill of lading, on the pallet tags and on the invoice, and the same code is the production record in Trazo, so an invoice traces back to the picks, the inputs and the parcel without anyone having to reconstruct it.

label_claim_review_process.value: I review anything that carries an organic claim before it is used — the clamshell film, the pallet tags, the bill of lading wording and, this year, the lot QR we started printing on the flats for OGC. New artwork goes to Oregon Tilth for label review before it is printed, which is what we did with the 2026 clamshell proof in June. Nothing goes on a package that is not on the certificate.

lot_numbering_description.value: Lot codes are CBF (Calapooia Bend Farm), the two-digit crop year, and the block abbreviation — CBF-26-HFE for Home Field East, CBF-26-HFW, CBF-26-RB, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach on Bottom Ground A, CBF-26-BGA-CA for the carrots that followed it, CBF-26-BGB, CBF-26-UT. Individual picks carry the lot plus the pick number (CBF-26-HFE-P1). Buffer-row fruit gets its own code ending -BUF so it can never be mistaken for the organic lot.

commingling_barriers.narrative:
[G6.0 Organic Production & Split Operations]
Split operation (organic and conventional production under the same management): No.
Parallel production (same crop grown organic and conventional): No.
Buffer and separation strategies used across the operation: Buffer-crop containers marked or kept separate — never marked organic; Buffer harvest stored apart from organic product; Buffer rows harvested at a different time than the organic crop; Buffer crop sold to a different buyer than the organic crop; Separate harvest and sales records kept for buffer crop; Buffer areas flagged or marked in the field.
Drift-prevention safeguards in place: Written notification to neighboring landowners or operators about the organic operation's location and boundaries; No-spray or advance-notice agreements with neighboring operators; Boundary signage marking the organic operation; Routine monitoring of adjoining land for spray activity or land-use changes; Awareness of wind conditions when neighbors are known to spray; Buffer-zone crop excluded from the organic harvest (see Buffer & separation strategy above); Documented procedure for logging suspected drift or contact incidents.
Response procedure when drift or contact with a prohibited substance is suspected: Stop harvest on the affected rows, isolate anything already picked, and photograph and note what was seen — wind, time, direction, the equipment on the neighbouring ground. Call Oregon Tilth the same day before any of that product moves, and follow their instruction on whether to test or to divert the block. Nothing from an affected area ships as organic until OTCO says it may. The neighbours on the north and west lines have standing written no-spray-without-notice agreements with us and both have honoured them since 2011.
Materials prohibited in organic production are kept on site: No.

[G6.1 Harvest & Transport]
Harvest is performed by: Our own crew.
Containers and bins used at harvest: Reusable lugs; Single-use cartons; Totes.
Containers are new, dedicated to organic use, or cleaned before each use: Yes.
Container cleaning method: The picking lugs are dedicated to organic fruit (buffer-row fruit goes into red-tagged lugs that are never used for an organic pick, section G6.0), and they are washed and sanitised before the first pick of each block: pressure wash, hand scrub, Tsunami 100 peroxyacetic acid at 80 ppm checked with test strips, then air dried on racks. The pack line is sanitised the same way the morning of each pack day. Both are logged as equipment cleanout records against the season.
Containers that previously held a prohibited substance are ever reused for organic product: No.
Packaging materials, storage containers, and bins free of synthetic fungicides, preservatives, and fumigants: Yes — confirmed with the supplier or from product documentation.
Product is transported off the operation by: Commercial carrier.
Transport units are inspected clean before loading organic product: Yes.
Every load leaves the operation with lot identification tying it to the field and harvest date: Yes.
Records provided by the carrier or handler transporting product off the operation: Organically Grown Company's reefer collects the fresh fruit. Every load leaves with a bill of lading carrying our lot code, the pallet count, the seal number and the words 'Certified organic — OTCO-1463', and the driver signs it. OGC returns a receiving report against the same lot. The trailer is pre-cooled and inspected before loading and the carrier attaches a cleanout affidavit naming the previous load. Willamette Valley Fruit collect the process fruit on the same terms, on their own separate BOL.

[G6.2 Storage]
Organic product is stored in: On-farm cold storage; On-farm dry storage.
Storage shared with nonorganic product: No.
Storage areas cleaned and inspected before organic product enters: Yes.
Cleaning and inspection method for storage areas: The cooler is emptied, swept, washed down and the floor and drains sanitised before the first fruit of the season goes in, and it is checked and wiped between crops. The onion shed is swept out and the forced-air fans and ducts cleaned before curing starts. Both are inspected by eye at the same time — for damp, for rodent sign, for anything left from the previous crop — and the check is written on the cleanout log.
Pest control materials used in storage areas: No.
Lot identity maintained through storage (bin cards, pallet tags): Yes.

[G6.4 On-Farm Handling]
Water source and sanitizer used in handling: Potable water from Well #1, tested annually (Edge Analytical, 2026 report 26-W-0412). Tsunami 100 (peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide) is dosed in the wash flume at 80 ppm and checked with test strips; it is allowed under § 205.601(a)(6). No chlorine is used, and residual is not an issue because there is no chlorine rinse step.
Commingling controls used during handling: Dedicated organic-only equipment; Facility handles organic product only; Labeled, dedicated containers throughout handling; Equipment cleanout between runs, with records.

[G7.0 Labeling]
Organic product leaves this operation as: Consumer-ready packaging with a printed organic label; Bulk bins or totes with container markings (no consumer label).
Organic product is sold under the following labeling categories: Organic.
Consumer label identifies the certifying agent: Yes.
USDA organic seal displayed on the label: Yes.
Sales documents identify organic shipments by lot number: Yes.
Container markings link to the same lot identification used in records: Yes.
New labels and organic claims are reviewed by: I review anything that carries an organic claim before it is used — the clamshell film, the pallet tags, the bill of lading wording and, this year, the lot QR we started printing on the flats for OGC. New artwork goes to Oregon Tilth for label review before it is printed, which is what we did with the 2026 clamshell proof in June. Nothing goes on a package that is not on the certificate.

The neighbours on the north and west lines have standing written no-spray-without-notice agreements with us and both have honoured them since 2011.
Materials prohibited in organic production are kept on site: No.

[G6.1 Harvest & Transport]
Harvest is performed by: Our own crew.
Containers and bins used at harvest: Reusable lugs; Single-use cartons; Totes.
Containers are new, dedicated to organic use, or cleaned before each use: Yes.
Container cleaning method: The picking lugs are dedicated to organic fruit (buffer-row fruit goes into red-tagged lugs that are never used for an organic pick, section G6.0), and they are washed and sanitised before the first pick of each block: pressure wash, hand scrub, Tsunami 100 peroxyacetic acid at 80 ppm checked with test strips, then air dried on racks. The pack line is sanitised the same way the morning of each pack day. Both are logged as equipment cleanout records against the season.
Containers that previously held a prohibited substance are ever reused for organic product: No.
Packaging materials, storage containers, and bins free of synthetic fungicides, preservatives, and fumigants: Yes — confirmed with the supplier or from product documentation.
Product is transported off the operation by: Commercial carrier.
Transport units are inspected clean before loading organic product: Yes.
Every load leaves the operation with lot identification tying it to the field and harvest date: Yes.
Records provided by the carrier or handler transporting product off the operation: Organically Grown Company's reefer collects the fresh fruit. Every load leaves with a bill of lading carrying our lot code, the pallet count, the seal number and the words 'Certified organic — OTCO-1463', and the driver signs it. OGC returns a receiving report against the same lot. The trailer is pre-cooled and inspected before loading and the carrier attaches a cleanout affidavit naming the previous load. Willamette Valley Fruit collect the process fruit on the same terms, on their own separate BOL.

[G6.2 Storage]
Organic product is stored in: On-farm cold storage; On-farm dry storage.
Storage shared with nonorganic product: No.
Storage areas cleaned and inspected before organic product enters: Yes.
Cleaning and inspection method for storage areas: The cooler is emptied, swept, washed down and the floor and drains sanitised before the first fruit of the season goes in, and it is checked and wiped between crops. The onion shed is swept out and the forced-air fans and ducts cleaned before curing starts. Both are inspected by eye at the same time — for damp, for rodent sign, for anything left from the previous crop — and the check is written on the cleanout log.
Pest control materials used in storage areas: No.
Lot identity maintained through storage (bin cards, pallet tags): Yes.

[G6.4 On-Farm Handling]
Water source and sanitizer used in handling: Potable water from Well #1, tested annually (Edge Analytical, 2026 report 26-W-0412). Tsunami 100 (peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide) is dosed in the wash flume at 80 ppm and checked with test strips; it is allowed under § 205.601(a)(6). No chlorine is used, and residual is not an issue because there is no chlorine rinse step.
Commingling controls used during handling: Dedicated organic-only equipment; Facility handles organic product only; Labeled, dedicated containers throughout handling; Equipment cleanout between runs, with records.

[G7.0 Labeling]
Organic product leaves this operation as: Consumer-ready packaging with a printed organic label; Bulk bins or totes with container markings (no consumer label).
Organic product is sold under the following labeling categories: Organic.
Consumer label identifies the certifying agent: Yes.
USDA organic seal displayed on the label: Yes.
Sales documents identify organic shipments by lot number: Yes.
Container markings link to the same lot identification used in records: Yes.
New labels and organic claims are reviewed by: I review anything that carries an organic claim before it is used — the clamshell film, the pallet tags, the bill of lading wording and, this year, the lot QR we started printing on the flats for OGC. New artwork goes to Oregon Tilth for label review before it is printed, which is what we did with the 2026 clamshell proof in June. Nothing goes on a package that is not on the certificate.

monitoring_plan.narrative:
[G2.0 Monitoring & Organic Fraud Prevention]
Identified organic fraud risk areas: We buy inputs, seed, or planting stock from uncertified suppliers; Custom harvesters, haulers, or hullers handle our product; Seasonal or temporary crews, or high staff turnover.
Organic fraud prevention practices: Verify that supplier organic certificates are current and cover the product bought; Check suppliers in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including surrendered, suspended, or revoked status; Review labels and paperwork when product or inputs are received; Buy from known, long-standing suppliers; Train staff on organic handling and separation; Our buyers audit or visit our operation; Report suspected fraud to our certifier or the NOP.
Process for reviewing fraud vulnerabilities and updating prevention measures: I review this myself each January when I put the renewal packet together, and again whenever something in the chain changes. The check is short because the chain is short: everything we sell is grown on our own six parcels and goes to two buyers — Organically Grown Company (OTCO-0042) for fresh, Willamette Valley Fruit for process. Before the first load of each season I pull both handlers' certificates and confirm they are current in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including that they have not been surrendered or suspended, and I do the same for any input supplier that is itself certified. Input labels and invoices are checked against the OSP materials list when the delivery lands, not later. The picking crew gets the organic-handling talk before harvest every year (see the June training record) because a seasonal crew is where separation actually gets tested — red-tagged buffer lugs, no personal produce in the field, clean lugs only. What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.
OSP review and update schedule: Annually at renewal; Whenever a practice, input, parcel, or supplier changes; Before each inspection.
Process for keeping the OSP accurate: Laurel Brandt, the owner, keeps the plan accurate. There are two of us who touch the records: Javier Morales logs the field work in Trazo as it happens — every spray, every pick, every cleanout — and I review what he has logged before the renewal packet goes to Oregon Tilth. A change on the ground reaches the plan by that route: when Grandevo went into the SWD rotation this February, it was logged as an input, the materials list changed, and OTCO got the change notice before the first application in June rather than after it. Anything that changes acreage, a parcel, a buyer or a handler goes to OTCO the same way.
Verification that OSP practices are implemented: Review the operation's records against the plan; Internal walk-through or self-audit; Staff training.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Fertility effectiveness monitored via: Soil tests; Leaf / tissue tests; Soil organic matter tracking; Crop health and yield observation.
Monitoring frequency: Annually.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Irrigation water sources: One well (Well #1, 25 hp submersible at 85 ft) supplies the whole farm — drip on all six parcels, with overhead only for germinating the vegetable ground. No surface water is drawn from the Calapooia and we are not on an irrigation district.
Irrigation water quality testing performed: Yes.
Water quality testing frequency: Annually before the season starts. Edge Analytical, Corvallis — 2026 report 26-W-0412 dated 20 May: generic E. coli <1 MPN/100 mL, nitrate-N 1.2 mg/L, pH 6.9.
Irrigation water supplied by a district or shared system: No.
Natural-resource outcomes are monitored through: Visual field checks.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease monitoring covers: Pest populations; Disease pressure; Weed pressure; Beneficial insect and natural predator activity.
Monitoring frequency: Weekly.
Monitoring results are recorded: Every scouting trip, trap read and threshold call is logged in Trazo against the block it belongs to, with the counts, what was found and what we decided — including the trips where we decided to do nothing, which are the majority. Trap positions are marked on the block map and the paper log sheet lives in the scouting binder in the office. The record for each application names the product, the rate, the area, the applicator and the REI and PHI.

[G6.5 Sales, Direct Marketing & Supplier Verification]
Sales channels: Wholesale only, two buyers. Organically Grown Company (Portland DC, handler certificate OTCO-0042) takes the fresh blueberries, the washed carrots, the sacked onions and the spinach. Willamette Valley Fruit takes the machine-picked process blueberries. We do not sell direct to consumers, we do not attend farmers' markets, and we run no CSA.
Purchase or resale of others' organic product: No — we sell only what we grow.
Sale-to-lot traceability: Every sale carries the lot code from the season it came out of — CBF-26-HFE for the Duke block, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach, and so on. The lot is on the bill of lading, on the pallet tags and on the invoice, and the same code is the production record in Trazo, so an invoice traces back to the picks, the inputs and the parcel without anyone having to reconstruct it.

practices_procedures.narrative:
[G3.0 Seeds & Planting Stock]
Seeds used in organic production: Organic, untreated; Non-organic, untreated.
Annual seedlings: Purchased certified organic seedlings (organic certificate kept for each supplier).
Planting stock: Non-organic.
Commercial-availability searches before non-organic seed use: Yes — searches are documented (source names, dates, and the characteristics evaluated).
Non-GMO status documented via: Non-GMO statement from the supplier; Seed tag kept on file; Catalog or label statement.
Grafting of planting stock: No.

[G3.0b Perennial Planting Stock]
Perennial planting stock established: Bare-root trees or vines; Containerized trees or vines.
Organic status of planting stock established: All nonorganic.
Planting stock sources and planting record: The blueberry plantings are the only perennial stock on the farm. Home Field East (12.5 ac 'Duke') was planted spring 2006 with two-year bare-root plants from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, Lowell OR. Home Field West (14.0 ac 'Draper') was planted spring 2013 with containerised plants from the same nursery. River Block (11.2 ac 'Liberty') was planted spring 2016, containerised, also Fall Creek. No perennial stock has been established since 2016 and none is planned. All three blocks are on raised beds with Douglas-fir sawdust mulch and drip.
Planting stock suppliers listed on the Supplier List: Yes.
Justification for nonorganic perennial planting stock: The variety or cultivar is not offered organically; Not available in the quantity needed.
Commercial availability search records kept: Nursery quotes or order confirmations; Emails with suppliers; Phone log of suppliers contacted.
Treatment of nonorganic planting stock: No — confirmed in writing by the nursery.
Perennial planting stock sold as organic: No — we sell only the harvested crop, never the plants.
Planting stock records kept: Nursery invoices or receipts; Variety and rootstock tags or labels; Planting map showing which block each lot went into; Written nursery statements about treatments applied.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Crop rotation plan (annual crops): The three vegetable parcels run a four-year rotation and never carry the same family twice running. Bottom Ground A: carrots 2025, spring spinach then a second carrot crop 2026, brassica 2027, then a full cover year. Bottom Ground B: onions 2025, carrots 2026, spinach 2027, cover 2028. Upper Terrace came out of a fallow/cover year in 2024 and went into onions in 2026 — it is the ground we rest when a block needs it. Every vegetable parcel carries a winter cover of cereal rye with hairy vetch and crimson clover, drilled behind the harvester in October and terminated in March or April. The blueberry blocks are perennial and are not rotated; biological diversity there comes from the permanent grass row middles, the hedgerow and the flowering understorey rather than from rotation.
Biological diversity in lieu of rotation: Permanent or seasonal ground cover; Cover crops between rows; Hedgerows or insectary plantings.
Soil fertility is managed through: Incorporation of crop residue; Cover crops / green manures; Compost; Plant materials / mulches; Mined minerals (gypsum, limestone); Side-dress or drip (fertigation) applications; Crop rotation.
Tillage and cultivation practices: Vegetable ground only. In autumn the crop residue is flail-mowed and disced in and the cover is drilled the same week. In March or April the cover is flailed at rye boot stage and disced in two passes, then the beds are rototilled to about six inches and levelled with a Perfecta harrow for seeding — that is the deepest we go, and it happens once per crop. In season the only steel in the ground is the finger and torsion weeders either side of the rows and bed-middle sweeps, both shallow. Nothing is inverted, we do not plough, and passes run across the slope. The blueberry blocks are not tilled at all: the row middles are permanent sod that is mown, and the under-row strip is mulched with sawdust.
Erosion is controlled through: Cover cropping; No-till or permanent cover; Contour farming or terraces; Conservation (minimum) tillage; Micro-irrigation management; Windbreaks.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Soil and water conservation practices used on this operation: Cover cropping; Reduced or minimum tillage; Riparian buffers; Irrigation efficiency improvements; Windbreaks.
Habitat and biodiversity practices used on this operation: Hedgerows; Native plantings; Pollinator habitat; Owl or raptor boxes or perches; Bat boxes; Wetland or woodland protection.
Conservation plans or agreements in place: Federal conservation agency (NRCS, FSA).
Conservation plan detail: NRCS EQIP contract covering practice 422 (field border) — the 1,400 ft native hedgerow along the Upper Terrace north edge, planted 2024 with oceanspray, red-flowering currant, snowberry and native rose. The same contract covers the pollinator strip on the Bottom Ground A headland. Linn Soil and Water Conservation District advised on the riparian corridor along the Calapooia on the east side of Bottom Ground A, which we leave uncut.
Invasive species prevention and control: Crew can identify the invasive species of concern locally; New infestations are monitored for and removed promptly; Competitive native plantings established in their place; Seed, planting stock, amendments and mulch sourced weed- and pest-free.
Wildlife and habitat pressures on this operation: Neither — no wildlife exclusion and no habitat converted since certification.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease prevention practices used: Crop rotation; Sanitation — removing crop residue, cull piles, and disease vectors; Cleaning tools and equipment between fields or blocks; Habitat for beneficial insects and natural predators (hedgerows, insectary plantings, refuge strips); Resistant or site-adapted plant varieties; Plant spacing and planting-date timing to reduce pest and disease pressure; Pruning and canopy management to improve airflow and reduce disease pressure; Mulching.
Crop residue is burned on this operation: No.
Weeds are managed through: Mechanical cultivation; Hand weeding; Mowing; Organic (biodegradable) mulch; Flame, heat, or electrical weeding; Cover-crop suppression (planted or roller-crimped covers that outcompete weeds).
Plastic or synthetic mulch used for weed control: No.
Allowed input materials are applied for pest, weed, or disease control when prevention is insufficient: Yes.
Conditions documented for applying allowed pest, weed, or disease control materials: Only when monitoring says prevention has not held, and only from the approved inputs list. On blueberries that means spotted wing drosophila: traps go up at green fruit and the first confirmed female once fruit shows colour is the action point, because SWD turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly threshold would be too late. The programme is then Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation, both OMRI listed, at four to five day pick intervals, applied at dusk after bee flight, with drops and culls buried the same day. Bloom disease is covered by Serenade Opti at about 30 percent bloom and again ten days later, only in a wet bloom. Surround WP goes on if we get a heat event at colour. On the vegetable ground no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied — weeds are handled by flaming, cultivation and hand crews. Nothing is applied while hives are on the block.

[G6.4 On-Farm Handling]
On-farm handling activities performed: Washing / rinsing; Sorting, grading, or sizing; Packing into consumer or nonretail containers; Cooling / hydrocooling.
Crops and product forms handled on-farm: Only what we grow: fresh blueberries in 12 x 1 pt clamshell flats, process blueberries in bulk totes, carrots washed and packed 25 lb, onions cured and sacked 50 lb, spinach washed, iced and packed 20 lb.
On-farm handling covers: Only our own crop.
Buildings, pads, and equipment used for on-farm handling: A single open-sided packing shed on the home place with a concrete floor, next to the two forced-air cooling tunnels and the cold room. The line is a wash tank and flume for the root and leaf crops, a roller sorting table, a grading belt and a clamshell filler for the fruit. The onion curing shed is separate, with forced-air fans. All of it is organic-only: buffer-row fruit never enters the shed, the cooler room or the pack line (section G6.0).
On-farm handling process, in order from harvest to shipment: Blueberries: hand picked into lugs, shuttled to the shed every 45 minutes, forced-air cooled to 34 F within two hours, tipped onto the sorting table, filled into clamshells, palletised with the lot code on the pallet tag, held at 34-35 F, shipped to OGC. Machine-picked tail fruit goes straight into totes and to Willamette Valley Fruit as process grade. Carrots: lifted, flumed and washed in well water, graded, packed 25 lb, cooled, shipped. Onions: lifted, field cured five days in the windrow, three weeks forced-air in the shed, topped, graded, sacked 50 lb. Spinach: band cut, flumed, iced and packed 20 lb the same day. Buffer-row fruit never enters this flow — it is picked separately into red-tagged lugs and goes out on its own bill of lading as conventional.
Water used in washing, rinsing, or hydrocooling: Yes.

[G9.0 Facility Pest Management]
Contracted pest control company used: No.
Facility pest prevention practices: Sanitation — cleaning up spilled product, culls, and debris; Removing pest habitat, food sources, and breeding areas; Exclusion — sealing gaps, screens, door sweeps, air curtains; Managing temperature, humidity, or light to discourage pests; Routine monitoring and inspection of the structure.
Mechanical and physical facility pest controls: Traps; Barriers or screens.
Facility pest control materials used: None are used.

[W2.0 Wild Crop Harvesting]
Not applicable — reviewed and attested by the operator on 2026-08-21.

Bottom Ground A: carrots 2025, spring spinach then a second carrot crop 2026, brassica 2027, then a full cover year. Bottom Ground B: onions 2025, carrots 2026, spinach 2027, cover 2028. Upper Terrace came out of a fallow/cover year in 2024 and went into onions in 2026 — it is the ground we rest when a block needs it. Every vegetable parcel carries a winter cover of cereal rye with hairy vetch and crimson clover, drilled behind the harvester in October and terminated in March or April. The blueberry blocks are perennial and are not rotated; biological diversity there comes from the permanent grass row middles, the hedgerow and the flowering understorey rather than from rotation.
Biological diversity in lieu of rotation: Permanent or seasonal ground cover; Cover crops between rows; Hedgerows or insectary plantings.
Soil fertility is managed through: Incorporation of crop residue; Cover crops / green manures; Compost; Plant materials / mulches; Mined minerals (gypsum, limestone); Side-dress or drip (fertigation) applications; Crop rotation.
Tillage and cultivation practices: Vegetable ground only. In autumn the crop residue is flail-mowed and disced in and the cover is drilled the same week. In March or April the cover is flailed at rye boot stage and disced in two passes, then the beds are rototilled to about six inches and levelled with a Perfecta harrow for seeding — that is the deepest we go, and it happens once per crop. In season the only steel in the ground is the finger and torsion weeders either side of the rows and bed-middle sweeps, both shallow. Nothing is inverted, we do not plough, and passes run across the slope. The blueberry blocks are not tilled at all: the row middles are permanent sod that is mown, and the under-row strip is mulched with sawdust.
Erosion is controlled through: Cover cropping; No-till or permanent cover; Contour farming or terraces; Conservation (minimum) tillage; Micro-irrigation management; Windbreaks.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Soil and water conservation practices used on this operation: Cover cropping; Reduced or minimum tillage; Riparian buffers; Irrigation efficiency improvements; Windbreaks.
Habitat and biodiversity practices used on this operation: Hedgerows; Native plantings; Pollinator habitat; Owl or raptor boxes or perches; Bat boxes; Wetland or woodland protection.
Conservation plans or agreements in place: Federal conservation agency (NRCS, FSA).
Conservation plan detail: NRCS EQIP contract covering practice 422 (field border) — the 1,400 ft native hedgerow along the Upper Terrace north edge, planted 2024 with oceanspray, red-flowering currant, snowberry and native rose. The same contract covers the pollinator strip on the Bottom Ground A headland. Linn Soil and Water Conservation District advised on the riparian corridor along the Calapooia on the east side of Bottom Ground A, which we leave uncut.
Invasive species prevention and control: Crew can identify the invasive species of concern locally; New infestations are monitored for and removed promptly; Competitive native plantings established in their place; Seed, planting stock, amendments and mulch sourced weed- and pest-free.
Wildlife and habitat pressures on this operation: Neither — no wildlife exclusion and no habitat converted since certification.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease prevention practices used: Crop rotation; Sanitation — removing crop residue, cull piles, and disease vectors; Cleaning tools and equipment between fields or blocks; Habitat for beneficial insects and natural predators (hedgerows, insectary plantings, refuge strips); Resistant or site-adapted plant varieties; Plant spacing and planting-date timing to reduce pest and disease pressure; Pruning and canopy management to improve airflow and reduce disease pressure; Mulching.
Crop residue is burned on this operation: No.
Weeds are managed through: Mechanical cultivation; Hand weeding; Mowing; Organic (biodegradable) mulch; Flame, heat, or electrical weeding; Cover-crop suppression (planted or roller-crimped covers that outcompete weeds).
Plastic or synthetic mulch used for weed control: No.
Allowed input materials are applied for pest, weed, or disease control when prevention is insufficient: Yes.
Conditions documented for applying allowed pest, weed, or disease control materials: Only when monitoring says prevention has not held, and only from the approved inputs list. On blueberries that means spotted wing drosophila: traps go up at green fruit and the first confirmed female once fruit shows colour is the action point, because SWD turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly threshold would be too late. The programme is then Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation, both OMRI listed, at four to five day pick intervals, applied at dusk after bee flight, with drops and culls buried the same day. Bloom disease is covered by Serenade Opti at about 30 percent bloom and again ten days later, only in a wet bloom. Surround WP goes on if we get a heat event at colour. On the vegetable ground no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied — weeds are handled by flaming, cultivation and hand crews. Nothing is applied while hives are on the block.

[G6.4 On-Farm Handling]
On-farm handling activities performed: Washing / rinsing; Sorting, grading, or sizing; Packing into consumer or nonretail containers; Cooling / hydrocooling.
Crops and product forms handled on-farm: Only what we grow: fresh blueberries in 12 x 1 pt clamshell flats, process blueberries in bulk totes, carrots washed and packed 25 lb, onions cured and sacked 50 lb, spinach washed, iced and packed 20 lb.
On-farm handling covers: Only our own crop.
Buildings, pads, and equipment used for on-farm handling: A single open-sided packing shed on the home place with a concrete floor, next to the two forced-air cooling tunnels and the cold room. The line is a wash tank and flume for the root and leaf crops, a roller sorting table, a grading belt and a clamshell filler for the fruit. The onion curing shed is separate, with forced-air fans. All of it is organic-only: buffer-row fruit never enters the shed, the cooler room or the pack line (section G6.0).
On-farm handling process, in order from harvest to shipment: Blueberries: hand picked into lugs, shuttled to the shed every 45 minutes, forced-air cooled to 34 F within two hours, tipped onto the sorting table, filled into clamshells, palletised with the lot code on the pallet tag, held at 34-35 F, shipped to OGC. Machine-picked tail fruit goes straight into totes and to Willamette Valley Fruit as process grade. Carrots: lifted, flumed and washed in well water, graded, packed 25 lb, cooled, shipped. Onions: lifted, field cured five days in the windrow, three weeks forced-air in the shed, topped, graded, sacked 50 lb. Spinach: band cut, flumed, iced and packed 20 lb the same day. Buffer-row fruit never enters this flow — it is picked separately into red-tagged lugs and goes out on its own bill of lading as conventional.
Water used in washing, rinsing, or hydrocooling: Yes.

Contracted pest control company used: No.
Facility pest prevention practices: Sanitation — cleaning up spilled product, culls, and debris; Removing pest habitat, food sources, and breeding areas; Exclusion — sealing gaps, screens, door sweeps, air curtains; Managing temperature, humidity, or light to discourage pests; Routine monitoring and inspection of the structure.
Mechanical and physical facility pest controls: Traps; Barriers or screens.
Facility pest control materials used: None are used.

Not applicable — reviewed and attested by the operator on 2026-08-21.

contract_notes.value: Brandt Family Farms LLC, an Oregon limited liability company, trading as Calapooia Bend Farm. fraud_review_process.value: I review this myself each January when I put the renewal packet together, and again whenever something in the chain changes. The check is short because the chain is short: everything we sell is grown on our own six parcels and goes to two buyers — Organically Grown Company (OTCO-0042) for fresh, Willamette Valley Fruit for process. Before the first load of each season I pull both handlers' certificates and confirm they are current in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including that they have not been surrendered or suspended, and I do the same for any input supplier that is itself certified. Input labels and invoices are checked against the OSP materials list when the delivery lands, not later. The picking crew gets the organic-handling talk before harvest every year (see the June training record) because a seasonal crew is where separation actually gets tested — red-tagged buffer lugs, no personal produce in the field, clean lugs only. What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.

osp_accuracy_process.value: Laurel Brandt, the owner, keeps the plan accurate. raw_manure_timing_detail.value: No raw manure is applied anywhere on this operation, and none is kept on the farm. They are distinguished at harvest by day (buffer rows are picked last, on their own day), by container (red-tagged lugs, organic-only lugs never touch buffer fruit), by lot code (CBF-26-HFE for the organic lot, CBF-26-HFE-BUF for the buffer), by destination (OGC takes the organic fruit as fresh; the buffer fruit goes to Willamette Valley Fruit as conventional process), and by paperwork — a separate weigh ticket, a separate bill of lading and a separate sales record, none of which carry the word organic. The 2026 buffer pick was 2,300 lb on 7 July, recorded as a Buffer Use activity with the disposition 'sold as conventional (documented)'.

Nothing else on the operation is non-organic: all 86.9 acres are certified, and no prohibited material is stored anywhere on the farm.

The pack line is sanitised the same way the morning of each pack day. Both are logged as equipment cleanout records against the season.

OGC returns a receiving report against the same lot. The trailer is pre-cooled and inspected before loading and the carrier attaches a cleanout affidavit naming the previous load. water_source_sanitizer.value: Potable water from Well #1, tested annually (Edge Analytical, 2026 report 26-W-0412). Tsunami 100 (peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide) is dosed in the wash flume at 80 ppm and checked with test strips; it is allowed under § 205.601(a)(6). sales_soe_lot_linkage.value: Every sale carries the lot code from the season it came out of — CBF-26-HFE for the Duke block, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach, and so on. label_claim_review_process.value: I review anything that carries an organic claim before it is used — the clamshell film, the pallet tags, the bill of lading wording and, this year, the lot QR we started printing on the flats for OGC. lot_numbering_description.value: Lot codes are CBF (Calapooia Bend Farm), the two-digit crop year, and the block abbreviation — CBF-26-HFE for Home Field East, CBF-26-HFW, CBF-26-RB, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach on Bottom Ground A, CBF-26-BGA-CA for the carrots that followed it, CBF-26-BGB, CBF-26-UT. Drift-prevention safeguards in place: Written notification to neighboring landowners or operators about the organic operation's location and boundaries; No-spray or advance-notice agreements with neighboring operators; Boundary signage marking the organic operation; Routine monitoring of adjoining land for spray activity or land-use changes; Awareness of wind conditions when neighbors are known to spray; Buffer-zone crop excluded from the organic harvest (see Buffer & separation strategy above); Documented procedure for logging suspected drift or contact incidents.

Product is transported off the operation by: Commercial carrier.
Transport units are inspected clean before loading organic product: Yes.
Every load leaves the operation with lot identification tying it to the field and harvest date: Yes.

monitoring_plan.narrative:
[G2.0 Monitoring & Organic Fraud Prevention]
Identified organic fraud risk areas: We buy inputs, seed, or planting stock from uncertified suppliers; Custom harvesters, haulers, or hullers handle our product; Seasonal or temporary crews, or high staff turnover.
Organic fraud prevention practices: Verify that supplier organic certificates are current and cover the product bought; Check suppliers in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including surrendered, suspended, or revoked status; Review labels and paperwork when product or inputs are received; Buy from known, long-standing suppliers; Train staff on organic handling and separation; Our buyers audit or visit our operation; Report suspected fraud to our certifier or the NOP.
Process for reviewing fraud vulnerabilities and updating prevention measures: I review this myself each January when I put the renewal packet together, and again whenever something in the chain changes. The check is short because the chain is short: everything we sell is grown on our own six parcels and goes to two buyers — Organically Grown Company (OTCO-0042) for fresh, Willamette Valley Fruit for process. Before the first load of each season I pull both handlers' certificates and confirm they are current in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including that they have not been surrendered or suspended, and I do the same for any input supplier that is itself certified. Input labels and invoices are checked against the OSP materials list when the delivery lands, not later. The picking crew gets the organic-handling talk before harvest every year (see the June training record) because a seasonal crew is where separation actually gets tested — red-tagged buffer lugs, no personal produce in the field, clean lugs only. What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.
OSP review and update schedule: Annually at renewal; Whenever a practice, input, parcel, or supplier changes; Before each inspection.
Process for keeping the OSP accurate: Laurel Brandt, the owner, keeps the plan accurate. There are two of us who touch the records: Javier Morales logs the field work in Trazo as it happens — every spray, every pick, every cleanout — and I review what he has logged before the renewal packet goes to Oregon Tilth. A change on the ground reaches the plan by that route: when Grandevo went into the SWD rotation this February, it was logged as an input, the materials list changed, and OTCO got the change notice before the first application in June rather than after it. Anything that changes acreage, a parcel, a buyer or a handler goes to OTCO the same way.
Verification that OSP practices are implemented: Review the operation's records against the plan; Internal walk-through or self-audit; Staff training.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Fertility effectiveness monitored via: Soil tests; Leaf / tissue tests; Soil organic matter tracking; Crop health and yield observation.
Monitoring frequency: Annually.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Irrigation water sources: One well (Well #1, 25 hp submersible at 85 ft) supplies the whole farm — drip on all six parcels, with overhead only for germinating the vegetable ground. No surface water is drawn from the Calapooia and we are not on an irrigation district.
Irrigation water quality testing performed: Yes.
Water quality testing frequency: Annually before the season starts. Edge Analytical, Corvallis — 2026 report 26-W-0412 dated 20 May: generic E. coli <1 MPN/100 mL, nitrate-N 1.2 mg/L, pH 6.9.
Irrigation water supplied by a district or shared system: No.
Natural-resource outcomes are monitored through: Visual field checks.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease monitoring covers: Pest populations; Disease pressure; Weed pressure; Beneficial insect and natural predator activity.
Monitoring frequency: Weekly.
Monitoring results are recorded: Every scouting trip, trap read and threshold call is logged in Trazo against the block it belongs to, with the counts, what was found and what we decided — including the trips where we decided to do nothing, which are the majority. Trap positions are marked on the block map and the paper log sheet lives in the scouting binder in the office. The record for each application names the product, the rate, the area, the applicator and the REI and PHI.

[G6.5 Sales, Direct Marketing & Supplier Verification]
Sales channels: Wholesale only, two buyers. Organically Grown Company (Portland DC, handler certificate OTCO-0042) takes the fresh blueberries, the washed carrots, the sacked onions and the spinach. Willamette Valley Fruit takes the machine-picked process blueberries. We do not sell direct to consumers, we do not attend farmers' markets, and we run no CSA.
Purchase or resale of others' organic product: No — we sell only what we grow.
Sale-to-lot traceability: Every sale carries the lot code from the season it came out of — CBF-26-HFE for the Duke block, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach, and so on. The lot is on the bill of lading, on the pallet tags and on the invoice, and the same code is the production record in Trazo, so an invoice traces back to the picks, the inputs and the parcel without anyone having to reconstruct it.

practices_procedures.narrative:
[G3.0 Seeds & Planting Stock]
Seeds used in organic production: Organic, untreated; Non-organic, untreated.
Annual seedlings: Purchased certified organic seedlings (organic certificate kept for each supplier).
Planting stock: Non-organic.
Commercial-availability searches before non-organic seed use: Yes — searches are documented (source names, dates, and the characteristics evaluated).
Non-GMO status documented via: Non-GMO statement from the supplier; Seed tag kept on file; Catalog or label statement.
Grafting of planting stock: No.

[G3.0b Perennial Planting Stock]
Perennial planting stock established: Bare-root trees or vines; Containerized trees or vines.
Organic status of planting stock established: All nonorganic.
Planting stock sources and planting record: The blueberry plantings are the only perennial stock on the farm. Home Field East (12.5 ac 'Duke') was planted spring 2006 with two-year bare-root plants from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, Lowell OR. Home Field West (14.0 ac 'Draper') was planted spring 2013 with containerised plants from the same nursery. River Block (11.2 ac 'Liberty') was planted spring 2016, containerised, also Fall Creek. No perennial stock has been established since 2016 and none is planned. All three blocks are on raised beds with Douglas-fir sawdust mulch and drip.
Planting stock suppliers listed on the Supplier List: Yes.
Justification for nonorganic perennial planting stock: The variety or cultivar is not offered organically; Not available in the quantity needed.
Commercial availability search records kept: Nursery quotes or order confirmations; Emails with suppliers; Phone log of suppliers contacted.
Treatment of nonorganic planting stock: No — confirmed in writing by the nursery.
Perennial planting stock sold as organic: No — we sell only the harvested crop, never the plants.
Planting stock records kept: Nursery invoices or receipts; Variety and rootstock tags or labels; Planting map showing which block each lot went into; Written nursery statements about treatments applied.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Crop rotation plan (annual crops): The three vegetable parcels run a four-year rotation and never carry the same family twice running. Bottom Ground A: carrots 2025, spring spinach then a second carrot crop 2026, brassica 2027, then a full cover year. Bottom Ground B: onions 2025, carrots 2026, spinach 2027, cover 2028. Upper Terrace came out of a fallow/cover year in 2024 and went into onions in 2026 — it is the ground we rest when a block needs it. Every vegetable parcel carries a winter cover of cereal rye with hairy vetch and crimson clover, drilled behind the harvester in October and terminated in March or April. The blueberry blocks are perennial and are not rotated; biological diversity there comes from the permanent grass row middles, the hedgerow and the flowering understorey rather than from rotation.
Biological diversity in lieu of rotation: Permanent or seasonal ground cover; Cover crops between rows; Hedgerows or insectary plantings.
Soil fertility is managed through: Incorporation of crop residue; Cover crops / green manures; Compost; Plant materials / mulches; Mined minerals (gypsum, limestone); Side-dress or drip (fertigation) applications; Crop rotation.
Tillage and cultivation practices: Vegetable ground only. In autumn the crop residue is flail-mowed and disced in and the cover is drilled the same week. In March or April the cover is flailed at rye boot stage and disced in two passes, then the beds are rototilled to about six inches and levelled with a Perfecta harrow for seeding — that is the deepest we go, and it happens once per crop. In season the only steel in the ground is the finger and torsion weeders either side of the rows and bed-middle sweeps, both shallow. Nothing is inverted, we do not plough, and passes run across the slope. The blueberry blocks are not tilled at all: the row middles are permanent sod that is mown, and the under-row strip is mulched with sawdust.
Erosion is controlled through: Cover cropping; No-till or permanent cover; Contour farming or terraces; Conservation (minimum) tillage; Micro-irrigation management; Windbreaks.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Soil and water conservation practices used on this operation: Cover cropping; Reduced or minimum tillage; Riparian buffers; Irrigation efficiency improvements; Windbreaks.
Habitat and biodiversity practices used on this operation: Hedgerows; Native plantings; Pollinator habitat; Owl or raptor boxes or perches; Bat boxes; Wetland or woodland protection.
Conservation plans or agreements in place: Federal conservation agency (NRCS, FSA).
Conservation plan detail: NRCS EQIP contract covering practice 422 (field border) — the 1,400 ft native hedgerow along the Upper Terrace north edge, planted 2024 with oceanspray, red-flowering currant, snowberry and native rose. The same contract covers the pollinator strip on the Bottom Ground A headland. Linn Soil and Water Conservation District advised on the riparian corridor along the Calapooia on the east side of Bottom Ground A, which we leave uncut.
Invasive species prevention and control: Crew can identify the invasive species of concern locally; New infestations are monitored for and removed promptly; Competitive native plantings established in their place; Seed, planting stock, amendments and mulch sourced weed- and pest-free.
Wildlife and habitat pressures on this operation: Neither — no wildlife exclusion and no habitat converted since certification.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease prevention practices used: Crop rotation; Sanitation — removing crop residue, cull piles, and disease vectors; Cleaning tools and equipment between fields or blocks; Habitat for beneficial insects and natural predators (hedgerows, insectary plantings, refuge strips); Resistant or site-adapted plant varieties; Plant spacing and planting-date timing to reduce pest and disease pressure; Pruning and canopy management to improve airflow and reduce disease pressure; Mulching.
Crop residue is burned on this operation: No.
Weeds are managed through: Mechanical cultivation; Hand weeding; Mowing; Organic (biodegradable) mulch; Flame, heat, or electrical weeding; Cover-crop suppression (planted or roller-crimped covers that outcompete weeds).
Plastic or synthetic mulch used for weed control: No.
Allowed input materials are applied for pest, weed, or disease control when prevention is insufficient: Yes.
Conditions documented for applying allowed pest, weed, or disease control materials: Only when monitoring says prevention has not held, and only from the approved inputs list. On blueberries that means spotted wing drosophila: traps go up at green fruit and the first confirmed female once fruit shows colour is the action point, because SWD turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly threshold would be too late. The programme is then Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation, both OMRI listed, at four to five day pick intervals, applied at dusk after bee flight, with drops and culls buried the same day. Bloom disease is covered by Serenade Opti at about 30 percent bloom and again ten days later, only in a wet bloom. Surround WP goes on if we get a heat event at colour. On the vegetable ground no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied — weeds are handled by flaming, cultivation and hand crews. Nothing is applied while hives are on the block.

Distinction between parallel organic and conventional lots at harvest and sale: Yes, in the strict sense: the buffer rows are the same crop and the same cultivars ('Duke' on Home Field East, 'Draper' on Home Field West) as the certified organic rows beside them, so the organic and non-organic lots are visually identical and must be told apart by handling and paperwork rather than by appearance. contract_notes.value: Brandt Family Farms LLC, an Oregon limited liability company, trading as Calapooia Bend Farm. The certificate is issued to Brandt Family Farms LLC; Calapooia Bend Farm is the farm name that appears on our bills of lading and on the buyer-facing pages, and both names are on file with Oregon Tilth. Laurel Brandt is the member-manager and the person responsible for this organic system plan. The operation holds 138.6 acres in Linn County, of which 86.9 acres across six parcels are in certified organic production — 37.7 acres of blueberries (Home Field East 12.5, Home Field West 14.0, River Block 11.2) and 49.2 acres of rotation ground (Bottom Ground A 18.6, Bottom Ground B 16.4, Upper Terrace 14.2). The balance is the riparian corridor along the Calapooia, the native hedgerows, the farmstead, the packing shed and the equipment yard; none of it is cropped. The only non-organic product is the fruit off buffer rows 1 and 2 on Home Field East and Home Field West, kept separate and sold as conventional process fruit as section G6.0 describes; no other crop on the operation is grown for the conventional market.

fraud_review_process.value: I review this myself each August when I put the annual update together, and again whenever something in the chain changes. The check is short because the chain is short: everything we sell is grown on our own six parcels and goes on our own reefer to two buyers: Organically Grown Company for fresh, Willamette Valley Fruit for processing. Before the first load of each season I pull both handlers' certificates and confirm they are current in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including that they have not been surrendered or suspended, and I do the same for any input supplier that is itself certified. Input labels and invoices are checked against the OSP materials list when the delivery lands, not later. The picking crew gets the organic-handling talk before harvest every year (see the June training record) because a seasonal crew is where separation actually gets tested — red-tagged buffer lugs, no personal produce in the field, clean lugs only. What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.

osp_accuracy_process.value: I keep the plan accurate (Laurel Brandt, member-manager). A change on the ground reaches the plan by that route: when Grandevo went into the SWD rotation this February, it was logged as an input, the materials list changed, and OTCO got the change notice before the first application in June rather than after it. Anything that changes acreage, a parcel, a buyer or a handler goes to OTCO the same way.

label_claim_review_process.value: I review anything that carries an organic claim before it is used — the clamshell film, the pallet tags, the bill of lading wording and, this year, the lot QR we started printing on the flats for OGC.
