commingling_barriers.narrative:
[G6.0 Organic Production & Split Operations]
Split operation (organic and conventional production under the same management): Yes.
Separation between organic and conventional production: The only non-organic product this farm produces is the fruit off the buffer rows, and § 205.202(c) is the reason it exists: rows 1 and 2 on the west edge of Home Field East and Home Field West sit against the county road and the neighbour's grass-seed ground, so their fruit cannot be sold as organic. It is kept separate at every step. The rows are staked orange and marked on the block map. They are picked on their own day, after the organic picks are finished, into red-tagged lugs that are not used for anything else. That fruit never enters the organic cooler room or the pack line — it goes straight onto a separate truck on its own bill of lading to Willamette Valley Fruit as conventional process fruit, with its own lot code ending -BUF and its own sales record. The crew is briefed on this at the pre-harvest meeting every season. Nothing else on the operation is non-organic: all 86.9 acres are certified, and no prohibited material is stored anywhere on the farm.
Parallel production (same crop grown organic and conventional): Yes.
Buffer and separation strategies used across the operation: Buffer-crop containers marked or kept separate — never marked organic; Buffer harvest stored apart from organic product; Buffer rows harvested at a different time than the organic crop; Buffer crop sold to a different buyer than the organic crop; Separate harvest and sales records kept for buffer crop; Buffer areas flagged or marked in the field.
Drift-prevention safeguards in place: Written notification to neighboring landowners or operators about the organic operation's location and boundaries; No-spray or advance-notice agreements with neighboring operators; Boundary signage marking the organic operation; Routine monitoring of adjoining land for spray activity or land-use changes; Awareness of wind conditions when neighbors are known to spray; Buffer-zone crop excluded from the organic harvest (see Buffer & separation strategy above); Documented procedure for logging suspected drift or contact incidents.
Response procedure when drift or contact with a prohibited substance is suspected: Stop harvest on the affected rows, isolate anything already picked, and photograph and note what was seen — wind, time, direction, the equipment on the neighbouring ground. Call Oregon Tilth the same day before any of that product moves, and follow their instruction on whether to test or to divert the block. Nothing from an affected area ships as organic until OTCO says it may. The neighbours on the north and west lines have standing written no-spray-without-notice agreements with us and both have honoured them since 2011.
Materials prohibited in organic production are kept on site: No.

[G6.1 Harvest & Transport]
Harvest is performed by: Our own crew.
Containers and bins used at harvest: Reusable lugs; Single-use cartons; Totes.
Containers are new, dedicated to organic use, or cleaned before each use: Yes.
Container cleaning method: The picking lugs are dedicated to organic fruit (buffer-row fruit goes into red-tagged lugs that are never used for an organic pick, section G6.0), and they are washed and sanitised before the first pick of each block: pressure wash, hand scrub, Tsunami 100 peroxyacetic acid at 80 ppm checked with test strips, then air dried on racks. The pack line is sanitised the same way the morning of each pack day. Both are logged as equipment cleanout records against the season.
Containers that previously held a prohibited substance are ever reused for organic product: No.
Packaging materials, storage containers, and bins free of synthetic fungicides, preservatives, and fumigants: Yes — confirmed with the supplier or from product documentation.
Product is transported off the operation by: Commercial carrier.
Transport units are inspected clean before loading organic product: Yes.
Every load leaves the operation with lot identification tying it to the field and harvest date: Yes.
Records provided by the carrier or handler transporting product off the operation: Organically Grown Company's reefer collects the fresh fruit. Every load leaves with a bill of lading carrying our lot code, the pallet count, the seal number and the words 'Certified organic — OTCO-1463', and the driver signs it. OGC returns a receiving report against the same lot. The trailer is pre-cooled and inspected before loading and the carrier attaches a cleanout affidavit naming the previous load. Willamette Valley Fruit collect the process fruit on the same terms, on their own separate BOL.

[G6.2 Storage]
Organic product is stored in: On-farm cold storage; On-farm dry storage.
Storage shared with nonorganic product: No.
Storage areas cleaned and inspected before organic product enters: Yes.
Cleaning and inspection method for storage areas: The cooler is emptied, swept, washed down and the floor and drains sanitised before the first fruit of the season goes in, and it is checked and wiped between crops. The onion shed is swept out and the forced-air fans and ducts cleaned before curing starts. Both are inspected by eye at the same time — for damp, for rodent sign, for anything left from the previous crop — and the check is written on the cleanout log.
Pest control materials used in storage areas: No.
Lot identity maintained through storage (bin cards, pallet tags): Yes.

[G6.4 On-Farm Handling]
Water source and sanitizer used in handling: Potable water from Well #1, tested annually (Edge Analytical, 2026 report 26-W-0412). Tsunami 100 (peroxyacetic acid and hydrogen peroxide) is dosed in the wash flume at 80 ppm and checked with test strips; it is allowed under § 205.601(a)(6). No chlorine is used, and residual is not an issue because there is no chlorine rinse step.
Commingling controls used during handling: Dedicated organic-only equipment; Facility handles organic product only; Labeled, dedicated containers throughout handling; Equipment cleanout between runs, with records.

[G7.0 Labeling]
Organic product leaves this operation as: Consumer-ready packaging with a printed organic label; Bulk bins or totes with container markings (no consumer label).
Organic product is sold under the following labeling categories: Organic.
Consumer label identifies the certifying agent: Yes.
USDA organic seal displayed on the label: Yes.
Sales documents identify organic shipments by lot number: Yes.
Container markings link to the same lot identification used in records: Yes.
New labels and organic claims are reviewed by: I review anything that carries an organic claim before it is used — the clamshell film, the pallet tags, the bill of lading wording and, this year, the lot QR we started printing on the flats for OGC. New artwork goes to Oregon Tilth for label review before it is printed, which is what we did with the 2026 clamshell proof in June. Nothing goes on a package that is not on the certificate.

monitoring_plan.narrative:
[G2.0 Monitoring & Organic Fraud Prevention]
Identified organic fraud risk areas: We buy inputs, seed, or planting stock from uncertified suppliers; Custom harvesters, haulers, or hullers handle our product; Seasonal or temporary crews, or high staff turnover.
Organic fraud prevention practices: Verify that supplier organic certificates are current and cover the product bought; Check suppliers in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including surrendered, suspended, or revoked status; Review labels and paperwork when product or inputs are received; Buy from known, long-standing suppliers; Train staff on organic handling and separation; Our buyers audit or visit our operation; Report suspected fraud to our certifier or the NOP.
Process for reviewing fraud vulnerabilities and updating prevention measures: I review this myself each January when I put the renewal packet together, and again whenever something in the chain changes. The check is short because the chain is short: everything we sell is grown on our own six parcels and goes to two buyers — Organically Grown Company (OTCO-0042) for fresh, Willamette Valley Fruit for process. Before the first load of each season I pull both handlers' certificates and confirm they are current in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, including that they have not been surrendered or suspended, and I do the same for any input supplier that is itself certified. Input labels and invoices are checked against the OSP materials list when the delivery lands, not later. The picking crew gets the organic-handling talk before harvest every year (see the June training record) because a seasonal crew is where separation actually gets tested — red-tagged buffer lugs, no personal produce in the field, clean lugs only. What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.
OSP review and update schedule: Annually at renewal; Whenever a practice, input, parcel, or supplier changes; Before each inspection.
Process for keeping the OSP accurate: Laurel Brandt, the owner, keeps the plan accurate. There are two of us who touch the records: Javier Morales logs the field work in Trazo as it happens — every spray, every pick, every cleanout — and I review what he has logged before the renewal packet goes to Oregon Tilth. A change on the ground reaches the plan by that route: when Grandevo went into the SWD rotation this February, it was logged as an input, the materials list changed, and OTCO got the change notice before the first application in June rather than after it. Anything that changes acreage, a parcel, a buyer or a handler goes to OTCO the same way.
Verification that OSP practices are implemented: Review the operation's records against the plan; Internal walk-through or self-audit; Staff training.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Fertility effectiveness monitored via: Soil tests; Leaf / tissue tests; Soil organic matter tracking; Crop health and yield observation.
Monitoring frequency: Annually.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Irrigation water sources: One well (Well #1, 25 hp submersible at 85 ft) supplies the whole farm — drip on all six parcels, with overhead only for germinating the vegetable ground. No surface water is drawn from the Calapooia and we are not on an irrigation district.
Irrigation water quality testing performed: Yes.
Water quality testing frequency: Annually before the season starts. Edge Analytical, Corvallis — 2026 report 26-W-0412 dated 20 May: generic E. coli <1 MPN/100 mL, nitrate-N 1.2 mg/L, pH 6.9.
Irrigation water supplied by a district or shared system: No.
Natural-resource outcomes are monitored through: Visual field checks.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease monitoring covers: Pest populations; Disease pressure; Weed pressure; Beneficial insect and natural predator activity.
Monitoring frequency: Weekly.
Monitoring results are recorded: Every scouting trip, trap read and threshold call is logged in Trazo against the block it belongs to, with the counts, what was found and what we decided — including the trips where we decided to do nothing, which are the majority. Trap positions are marked on the block map and the paper log sheet lives in the scouting binder in the office. The record for each application names the product, the rate, the area, the applicator and the REI and PHI.

[G6.5 Sales, Direct Marketing & Supplier Verification]
Sales channels: Wholesale only, two buyers. Organically Grown Company (Portland DC, handler certificate OTCO-0042) takes the fresh blueberries, the washed carrots, the sacked onions and the spinach. Willamette Valley Fruit takes the machine-picked process blueberries. We do not sell direct to consumers, we do not attend farmers' markets, and we run no CSA.
Purchase or resale of others' organic product: No — we sell only what we grow.
Sale-to-lot traceability: Every sale carries the lot code from the season it came out of — CBF-26-HFE for the Duke block, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach, and so on. The lot is on the bill of lading, on the pallet tags and on the invoice, and the same code is the production record in Trazo, so an invoice traces back to the picks, the inputs and the parcel without anyone having to reconstruct it.

What would make me change something: a new buyer or handler, a custom operator running their own equipment on our ground, a supplier whose certificate lapses, or a price that is too good for the product being offered. Anything I could not resolve would go to Oregon Tilth before the product moved.
OSP review and update schedule: Annually at renewal; Whenever a practice, input, parcel, or supplier changes; Before each inspection.
Process for keeping the OSP accurate: Laurel Brandt, the owner, keeps the plan accurate. There are two of us who touch the records: Javier Morales logs the field work in Trazo as it happens — every spray, every pick, every cleanout — and I review what he has logged before the renewal packet goes to Oregon Tilth. A change on the ground reaches the plan by that route: when Grandevo went into the SWD rotation this February, it was logged as an input, the materials list changed, and OTCO got the change notice before the first application in June rather than after it. Anything that changes acreage, a parcel, a buyer or a handler goes to OTCO the same way.
Verification that OSP practices are implemented: Review the operation's records against the plan; Internal walk-through or self-audit; Staff training.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Fertility effectiveness monitored via: Soil tests; Leaf / tissue tests; Soil organic matter tracking; Crop health and yield observation.
Monitoring frequency: Annually.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Irrigation water sources: One well (Well #1, 25 hp submersible at 85 ft) supplies the whole farm — drip on all six parcels, with overhead only for germinating the vegetable ground. No surface water is drawn from the Calapooia and we are not on an irrigation district.
Irrigation water quality testing performed: Yes.
Water quality testing frequency: Annually before the season starts. Edge Analytical, Corvallis — 2026 report 26-W-0412 dated 20 May: generic E. coli <1 MPN/100 mL, nitrate-N 1.2 mg/L, pH 6.9.
Irrigation water supplied by a district or shared system: No.
Natural-resource outcomes are monitored through: Visual field checks.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease monitoring covers: Pest populations; Disease pressure; Weed pressure; Beneficial insect and natural predator activity.
Monitoring frequency: Weekly.
Monitoring results are recorded: Every scouting trip, trap read and threshold call is logged in Trazo against the block it belongs to, with the counts, what was found and what we decided — including the trips where we decided to do nothing, which are the majority. Trap positions are marked on the block map and the paper log sheet lives in the scouting binder in the office. The record for each application names the product, the rate, the area, the applicator and the REI and PHI.

[G6.5 Sales, Direct Marketing & Supplier Verification]
Sales channels: Wholesale only, two buyers. Organically Grown Company (Portland DC, handler certificate OTCO-0042) takes the fresh blueberries, the washed carrots, the sacked onions and the spinach. Willamette Valley Fruit takes the machine-picked process blueberries. We do not sell direct to consumers, we do not attend farmers' markets, and we run no CSA.
Purchase or resale of others' organic product: No — we sell only what we grow.
Sale-to-lot traceability: Every sale carries the lot code from the season it came out of — CBF-26-HFE for the Duke block, CBF-26-BGA-SP for the spring spinach, and so on. The lot is on the bill of lading, on the pallet tags and on the invoice, and the same code is the production record in Trazo, so an invoice traces back to the picks, the inputs and the parcel without anyone having to reconstruct it.

practices_procedures.narrative:
[G3.0 Seeds & Planting Stock]
Seeds used in organic production: Organic, untreated; Non-organic, untreated.
Annual seedlings: Purchased certified organic seedlings (organic certificate kept for each supplier).
Planting stock: Non-organic.
Commercial-availability searches before non-organic seed use: Yes — searches are documented (source names, dates, and the characteristics evaluated).
Non-GMO status documented via: Non-GMO statement from the supplier; Seed tag kept on file; Catalog or label statement.
Grafting of planting stock: No.

[G3.0b Perennial Planting Stock]
Perennial planting stock established: Bare-root trees or vines; Containerized trees or vines.
Organic status of planting stock established: All nonorganic.
Planting stock sources and planting record: The blueberry plantings are the only perennial stock on the farm. Home Field East (12.5 ac 'Duke') was planted spring 2006 with two-year bare-root plants from Fall Creek Farm & Nursery, Lowell OR. Home Field West (14.0 ac 'Draper') was planted spring 2013 with containerised plants from the same nursery. River Block (11.2 ac 'Liberty') was planted spring 2016, containerised, also Fall Creek. No perennial stock has been established since 2016 and none is planned. All three blocks are on raised beds with Douglas-fir sawdust mulch and drip.
Planting stock suppliers listed on the Supplier List: Yes.
Justification for nonorganic perennial planting stock: The variety or cultivar is not offered organically; Not available in the quantity needed.
Commercial availability search records kept: Nursery quotes or order confirmations; Emails with suppliers; Phone log of suppliers contacted.
Treatment of nonorganic planting stock: No — confirmed in writing by the nursery.
Perennial planting stock sold as organic: No — we sell only the harvested crop, never the plants.
Planting stock records kept: Nursery invoices or receipts; Variety and rootstock tags or labels; Planting map showing which block each lot went into; Written nursery statements about treatments applied.

[G4.0 Rotation & Soil Management]
Crop rotation plan (annual crops): The three vegetable parcels run a four-year rotation and never carry the same family twice running. Bottom Ground A: carrots 2025, spring spinach then a second carrot crop 2026, brassica 2027, then a full cover year. Bottom Ground B: onions 2025, carrots 2026, spinach 2027, cover 2028. Upper Terrace came out of a fallow/cover year in 2024 and went into onions in 2026 — it is the ground we rest when a block needs it. Every vegetable parcel carries a winter cover of cereal rye with hairy vetch and crimson clover, drilled behind the harvester in October and terminated in March or April. The blueberry blocks are perennial and are not rotated; biological diversity there comes from the permanent grass row middles, the hedgerow and the flowering understorey rather than from rotation.
Biological diversity in lieu of rotation: Permanent or seasonal ground cover; Cover crops between rows; Hedgerows or insectary plantings.
Soil fertility is managed through: Incorporation of crop residue; Cover crops / green manures; Compost; Plant materials / mulches; Mined minerals (gypsum, limestone); Side-dress or drip (fertigation) applications; Crop rotation.
Tillage and cultivation practices: Vegetable ground only. In autumn the crop residue is flail-mowed and disced in and the cover is drilled the same week. In March or April the cover is flailed at rye boot stage and disced in two passes, then the beds are rototilled to about six inches and levelled with a Perfecta harrow for seeding — that is the deepest we go, and it happens once per crop. In season the only steel in the ground is the finger and torsion weeders either side of the rows and bed-middle sweeps, both shallow. Nothing is inverted, we do not plough, and passes run across the slope. The blueberry blocks are not tilled at all: the row middles are permanent sod that is mown, and the under-row strip is mulched with sawdust.
Erosion is controlled through: Cover cropping; No-till or permanent cover; Contour farming or terraces; Conservation (minimum) tillage; Micro-irrigation management; Windbreaks.

[G4.2 Natural Resources & Biodiversity]
Soil and water conservation practices used on this operation: Cover cropping; Reduced or minimum tillage; Riparian buffers; Irrigation efficiency improvements; Windbreaks.
Habitat and biodiversity practices used on this operation: Hedgerows; Native plantings; Pollinator habitat; Owl or raptor boxes or perches; Bat boxes; Wetland or woodland protection.
Conservation plans or agreements in place: Federal conservation agency (NRCS, FSA).
Conservation plan detail: NRCS EQIP contract covering practice 422 (field border) — the 1,400 ft native hedgerow along the Upper Terrace north edge, planted 2024 with oceanspray, red-flowering currant, snowberry and native rose. The same contract covers the pollinator strip on the Bottom Ground A headland. Linn Soil and Water Conservation District advised on the riparian corridor along the Calapooia on the east side of Bottom Ground A, which we leave uncut.
Invasive species prevention and control: Crew can identify the invasive species of concern locally; New infestations are monitored for and removed promptly; Competitive native plantings established in their place; Seed, planting stock, amendments and mulch sourced weed- and pest-free.
Wildlife and habitat pressures on this operation: Neither — no wildlife exclusion and no habitat converted since certification.

[G5.0 Crop Pest, Weed & Disease Management]
Pest, weed, and disease prevention practices used: Crop rotation; Sanitation — removing crop residue, cull piles, and disease vectors; Cleaning tools and equipment between fields or blocks; Habitat for beneficial insects and natural predators (hedgerows, insectary plantings, refuge strips); Resistant or site-adapted plant varieties; Plant spacing and planting-date timing to reduce pest and disease pressure; Pruning and canopy management to improve airflow and reduce disease pressure; Mulching.
Crop residue is burned on this operation: No.
Weeds are managed through: Mechanical cultivation; Hand weeding; Mowing; Organic (biodegradable) mulch; Flame, heat, or electrical weeding; Cover-crop suppression (planted or roller-crimped covers that outcompete weeds).
Plastic or synthetic mulch used for weed control: No.
Allowed input materials are applied for pest, weed, or disease control when prevention is insufficient: Yes.
Conditions documented for applying allowed pest, weed, or disease control materials: Only when monitoring says prevention has not held, and only from the approved inputs list. On blueberries that means spotted wing drosophila: traps go up at green fruit and the first confirmed female once fruit shows colour is the action point, because SWD turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly threshold would be too late. The programme is then Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation, both OMRI listed, at four to five day pick intervals, applied at dusk after bee flight, with drops and culls buried the same day. Bloom disease is covered by Serenade Opti at about 30 percent bloom and again ten days later, only in a wet bloom. Surround WP goes on if we get a heat event at colour. On the vegetable ground no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied — weeds are handled by flaming, cultivation and hand crews. No insecticide goes on while hives are on the block; the only bloom material is Serenade Opti (a biological fungicide), applied before 7 a.m. outside bee flight.

[G6.0 Organic Production & Split Operations]
Distinction between parallel organic and conventional lots at harvest and sale: Yes, in the strict sense: the buffer rows are the same crop and the same cultivars ('Duke' on Home Field East, 'Draper' on Home Field West) as the certified organic rows beside them, so the organic and non-organic lots are visually identical and must be told apart by handling and paperwork rather than by appearance. They are distinguished at harvest by day (buffer rows are picked last, on their own day), by container (red-tagged lugs, organic-only lugs never touch buffer fruit), by lot code (CBF-26-HFE for the organic lot, CBF-26-HFE-BUF for the buffer), by destination (OGC takes the organic fruit as fresh; the buffer fruit goes to Willamette Valley Fruit as conventional process), and by paperwork — a separate weigh ticket, a separate bill of lading and a separate sales record, none of which carry the word organic. The 2026 buffer pick was 2,300 lb on 7 July, recorded as a Buffer Use activity with the disposition 'sold as conventional (documented)'.

[G6.4 On-Farm Handling]
On-farm handling activities performed: Washing / rinsing; Sorting, grading, or sizing; Packing into consumer or nonretail containers; Cooling / hydrocooling.
Crops and product forms handled on-farm: Only what we grow: fresh blueberries in 12 x 1 pt clamshell flats, process blueberries in bulk totes, carrots washed and packed 25 lb, onions cured and sacked 50 lb, spinach washed, iced and packed 20 lb.
On-farm handling covers: Only our own crop.
Buildings, pads, and equipment used for on-farm handling: A single open-sided packing shed on the home place with a concrete floor, next to the two forced-air cooling tunnels and the cold room. The line is a wash tank and flume for the root and leaf crops, a roller sorting table, a grading belt and a clamshell filler for the fruit. The onion curing shed is separate, with forced-air fans. All of it is organic-only: buffer-row fruit never enters the shed, the cooler room or the pack line (section G6.0).
On-farm handling process, in order from harvest to shipment: Blueberries: hand picked into lugs, shuttled to the shed every 45 minutes, forced-air cooled to 34 F within two hours, tipped onto the sorting table, filled into clamshells, palletised with the lot code on the pallet tag, held at 34-35 F, shipped to OGC. Machine-picked tail fruit goes straight into totes and to Willamette Valley Fruit as process grade. Carrots: lifted, flumed and washed in well water, graded, packed 25 lb, cooled, shipped. Onions: lifted, field cured five days in the windrow, three weeks forced-air in the shed, topped, graded, sacked 50 lb. Spinach: band cut, flumed, iced and packed 20 lb the same day. Buffer-row fruit never enters this flow — it is picked separately into red-tagged lugs and goes out on its own bill of lading as conventional.
Water used in washing, rinsing, or hydrocooling: Yes.

[G9.0 Facility Pest Management]
Contracted pest control company used: No.
Facility pest prevention practices: Sanitation — cleaning up spilled product, culls, and debris; Removing pest habitat, food sources, and breeding areas; Exclusion — sealing gaps, screens, door sweeps, air curtains; Managing temperature, humidity, or light to discourage pests; Routine monitoring and inspection of the structure.
Mechanical and physical facility pest controls: Traps; Barriers or screens.
Facility pest control materials used: None are used.

[W2.0 Wild Crop Harvesting]
Not applicable — reviewed and attested by the operator on 2026-08-21.

seasons.description: Four picks, 118,750 lb off 12.5 acres — 9,500 lb/ac. Three hand picks fresh to OGC (100,900 lb picked, 97,066 lb packed out), last pick by machine to Willamette Valley Fruit as process grade (17,850 lb). Buffer row picked separately and sold conventional. Clean season: two Entrust, one Surround, no losses to SWD.

BusinessEvent.observation: Updated OTCO certificate received following the 2024 annual update: crops and handling scope, all six parcels, blueberries, carrots, onions, spinach. Certificate number unchanged.

Annual on-site inspection by the OTCO inspector: records, input storage, packing shed, buffers and the wash line. Walked Home Field East and Bottom Ground A. No noncompliances; one observation on labelling the sanitizer test-strip log, corrected on the spot.

ChemicalEvent.description: Rex Lime Sulfur application
ChemicalEvent.observation: Dormant lime sulfur at 10 gal/ac in 100 gal water, before bud swell, for mummy berry. Calm, 46 °F, dry for 24 h after.

ChemicalEvent.commercial_name: Down to Earth All Natural Fertilizers Feather Meal 12-0-0
ChemicalEvent.description: Down to Earth All Natural Fertilizers Feather Meal 12-0-0 application
ChemicalEvent.observation: Four hundred pounds per acre banded down the bed at bud break, 48 units of N. Slow release carries the bushes to fruit set; fish picks up after.

ChemicalEvent.observation: Entrust 1 of the season at 5 oz/ac, dawn, airblast at 100 gal/ac. Seven-day interval from the last; 3-day PHI held before the next pick. Season total kept inside the label limit.

PestManagementEvent.identification_method: Visual, 20 bushes per block, 5 clusters each
PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Blueberry program, in order: prevention first — permanent sod row middles and the hedgerow for beneficials, open canopy from dormant pruning, sanitation of drops and pack-line culls after every pick, and pick intervals held to four or five days. Monitoring: six Scentry SWD traps per block from green fruit, read Monday and Thursday, plus a weekly walk of twenty bushes per block with a beat tray. Threshold: the first confirmed SWD female once fruit shows color, because the fly turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly count would be read too late. Only then, materials: Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation (both OMRI listed), applied at dusk after bee flight, never while hives are on the block; Serenade Opti at bloom only in a wet bloom; Surround WP if a heat event lands at color. Everything applied is on the OSP inputs list.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Aphid colonies on new growth at the headland, below treatment level; no mummy berry cups found.

Threshold: the first confirmed SWD female once fruit shows color, because the fly turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly count would be read too late. Only then, materials: Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation (both OMRI listed), applied at dusk after bee flight, never while hives are on the block; Serenade Opti at bloom only in a wet bloom; Surround WP if a heat event lands at color. Everything applied is on the OSP inputs list.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Six apple-cider-vinegar traps, one per row band, serviced weekly. 3 male SWD this week.

PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Vegetable program, in order: prevention first — a four-year rotation that never repeats a family, a winter cover of rye with vetch and crimson clover on every vegetable parcel, and clean, certified organic seed. Weeds are handled mechanically, not chemically: flame weeding on the stale seedbed before emergence, then finger and torsion weeders at the two-leaf stage with a hand crew behind, then bed-middle sweeps until the canopy closes. Monitoring: a weekly walk with a sweep net, yellow sticky cards on the block edges for carrot rust fly, and roots pulled at ten points to check for tunnelling. Thresholds follow OSU Extension guidance; the cultural controls have held every season and no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied to the vegetable ground on this farm.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Leafminer stings low; aphid none. Downy mildew: none with the dry spring.

Threshold: the first confirmed SWD female once fruit shows color, because the fly turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly count would be read too late. Only then, materials: Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation (both OMRI listed), applied at dusk after bee flight, never while hives are on the block; Serenade Opti at bloom only in a wet bloom; Surround WP if a heat event lands at color. Everything applied is on the OSP inputs list.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Clean. Fruit set heavy.

SoilManagementEvent.amendment_product_name: Tiger 90CR elemental sulfur (90% S, degradable pastille)
SoilManagementEvent.amendment_supplier_name: Marion Ag Service, St. Paul OR
SoilManagementEvent.observation: Tiger 90CR at 300 lb/ac banded on the bed tops to hold pH near 5.0; last soil test read 5.3. Reacts over the season.
Twenty cores 0-8 in from the bed tops, composited by A&L Western. pH 5.3, OM 6.1%, CEC 12. Potassium a little low on this block; feather meal rate held, K from the fish.
Fifty recent fully-expanded leaves from fruiting laterals, mid-block, to A&L Western. N 1.95%, K 0.43% (low), B 28 ppm. Fall K from sulfate of potash-magnesia planned.

WeatherEvent.observation: Clear, calm, 29 °F at the orchard floor at 4 a.m. Overhead water ran on all blocks; no bloom loss found on the walk-through.
Three days 98-102 °F. Picked from first light and stopped by 11; drip sets lengthened; Surround film earned its keep. Some soft fruit on the west rows.

seasons.name: Draper 2025 — Home Field West

seasons.description: Four picks, 112,000 lb off 11.2 acres — 10,000 lb/ac despite the 14 June hail (about six percent marked, went process). Three hand picks fresh to OGC (91,000 lb picked, 87,542 lb packed out), machine pick to WVF (21,000 lb). Three Entrust. ROP inspection on the block 12 August.

BusinessEvent.observation: ROP add-on inspection: soil-grown confirmed on all blocks, no hydroponic or container production, pasture not applicable. Certificate renewed to June 2027.

PestManagementEvent.identification_method: Yellow sticky cards on margins (6), visual
PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Vegetable program, in order: prevention first — a four-year rotation that never repeats a family, a winter cover of rye with vetch and crimson clover on every vegetable parcel, and clean, certified organic seed. Weeds are handled mechanically, not chemically: flame weeding on the stale seedbed before emergence, then finger and torsion weeders at the two-leaf stage with a hand crew behind, then bed-middle sweeps until the canopy closes. Monitoring: a weekly walk with a sweep net, yellow sticky cards on the block edges for carrot rust fly, and roots pulled at ten points to check for tunnelling. Thresholds follow OSU Extension guidance; the cultural controls have held every season and no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied to the vegetable ground on this farm.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Carrot rust fly sticky traps out on the margins; none caught. Aster leafhopper present, low.
PestManagementEvent.pest_species: Psila rosae (carrot rust fly); Alternaria dauci

PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Vegetable program, in order: prevention first — a four-year rotation that never repeats a family, a winter cover of rye with vetch and crimson clover on every vegetable parcel, and clean, certified organic seed. Weeds are handled mechanically, not chemically: flame weeding on the stale seedbed before emergence, then finger and torsion weeders at the two-leaf stage with a hand crew behind, then bed-middle sweeps until the canopy closes. Monitoring: a weekly walk with a sweep net, yellow sticky cards on the block edges for carrot rust fly, and roots pulled at ten points to check for tunnelling. Thresholds follow OSU Extension guidance; the cultural controls have held every season and no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied to the vegetable ground on this farm.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Onion thrips: 2 per plant on the hot west edge, below threshold (OSU: 30/plant). Lady beetles present.

ProductionEvent.observation: Organic Patterson transplants from Calapooia Starts Co., Brownsville — 288-cell trays, four rows per bed, 4 in in-row, mechanical transplanter with a crew of ten. About 130,000 plants per acre.
Finger weeders in-row, knives between rows; hand crew behind.
Second pass, beds clean.
Third pass; some lambsquarters by hand.
Last pass before the tops fall; clean.
Drip tape from transplanting, 1-2 in a week on tensiometers, cut off 1 August to let the tops fall and the necks dry. About 13 in over the season.

Undercut and lifted with the bed lifter when 80 percent of the tops were down, 393,600 lb field weight estimated over the trailer scale on the first loads. Left in the field to cure five days in the windrow under a dry forecast.

Picked up from the windrow into bins and moved to the onion shed, forced-air at ambient for three weeks to finish the necks, then topped on the line and sacked 50 lb mesh as orders came in through October. Culls and small to the compost row. Pack-out about 85 percent.

PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Blueberry program, in order: prevention first — permanent sod row middles and the hedgerow for beneficials, open canopy from dormant pruning, sanitation of drops and pack-line culls after every pick, and pick intervals held to four or five days. Monitoring: six Scentry SWD traps per block from green fruit, read Monday and Thursday, plus a weekly walk of twenty bushes per block with a beat tray. Threshold: the first confirmed SWD female once fruit shows color, because the fly turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly count would be read too late. Only then, materials: Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation (both OMRI listed), applied at dusk after bee flight, never while hives are on the block; Serenade Opti at bloom only in a wet bloom; Surround WP if a heat event lands at color. Everything applied is on the OSP inputs list.

PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Blueberry program, in order: prevention first — permanent sod row middles and the hedgerow for beneficials, open canopy from dormant pruning, sanitation of drops and pack-line culls after every pick, and pick intervals held to four or five days. Monitoring: six Scentry SWD traps per block from green fruit, read Monday and Thursday, plus a weekly walk of twenty bushes per block with a beat tray. Threshold: the first confirmed SWD female once fruit shows color, because the fly turns a generation in about a week and a per-fly count would be read too late. Only then, materials: Entrust SC and Grandevo WDG in rotation (both OMRI listed), applied at dusk after bee flight, never while hives are on the block; Serenade Opti at bloom only in a wet bloom; Surround WP if a heat event lands at color. Everything applied is on the OSP inputs list.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Six ACV traps serviced weekly. 4 male SWD this week.

PestManagementEvent.identification_method: Yellow sticky cards on margins (6), visual
PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Vegetable program, in order: prevention first — a four-year rotation that never repeats a family, a winter cover of rye with vetch and crimson clover on every vegetable parcel, and clean, certified organic seed. Weeds are handled mechanically, not chemically: flame weeding on the stale seedbed before emergence, then finger and torsion weeders at the two-leaf stage with a hand crew behind, then bed-middle sweeps until the canopy closes. Monitoring: a weekly walk with a sweep net, yellow sticky cards on the block edges for carrot rust fly, and roots pulled at ten points to check for tunnelling. Thresholds follow OSU Extension guidance; the cultural controls have held every season and no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied to the vegetable ground on this farm.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Rust fly sticky cards out on the margins; none caught.
PestManagementEvent.pest_species: Psila rosae (carrot rust fly); Alternaria dauci

PestManagementEvent.ipm_strategy: Vegetable program, in order: prevention first — a four-year rotation that never repeats a family, a winter cover of rye with vetch and crimson clover on every vegetable parcel, and clean, certified organic seed. Weeds are handled mechanically, not chemically: flame weeding on the stale seedbed before emergence, then finger and torsion weeders at the two-leaf stage with a hand crew behind, then bed-middle sweeps until the canopy closes. Monitoring: a weekly walk with a sweep net, yellow sticky cards on the block edges for carrot rust fly, and roots pulled at ten points to check for tunnelling. Thresholds follow OSU Extension guidance; the cultural controls have held every season and no insecticide, fungicide or herbicide has ever been applied to the vegetable ground on this farm.
PestManagementEvent.observation: Onion thrips 1-2 per plant on the north edge by the hedgerow — well below threshold; lacewings on the hedgerow shrubs.
